newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Cheserem sees no drop in interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Cheserem sees no drop in interest rates.

text.p: Kenya's chief banker said on Thursday he saw no immediate fall in interest rates because his major near-term goal remained keeping inflation down.

"I make no apologies for this. My target is to keep inflation below 10 percent, and I am glad we have kept it there," Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem told a gathering of the American Business Association (in Kenya).
At last week's auction, the central bank offered an average interest rate of 14.990 percent on 28-day bills, 22.721 percent on 91-day bills and 20.070 percent interest on 182-day bills.
Commercial bank base lending rates range from 20-30 percent on average, but sometimes banks charge higher than that.
Inflation has risen in recent months. The central bank posted average annual inflation at 7.1 percent in August compared to 6.2 percent in July and 5.2 percent in June.
It posted three-month annualised inflation at 18.5 percent in August from 20.1 percent in July and 15.3 percent in June.

"We will reduce (interest rates) when the monetary environment permits. We are paying for the 1992/93 troubles," Cheserem said, referring to the government's printing of money for elections in 1992 that fuelled inflation to 101 percent.
"That will never happen again," he said.

Cheserem said the high cash ratio demanded from commercial banks by the central bank and high interest rates on government bills were partly to blame for the high rates but were crucial in keeping the infation down to a single digit.
Cash ratio is the amount of money each commercial bank must deposit with the central bank at no interest at all, and it currently stands at 18 percent.

Other causes for high interest rates included a high cost base for commercial banks, factoring of "bad debts" and a perception among commercial banks in Kenya they can only survive by making "super profits," he said.
"There is also high demand for credit from both the private sector and the government. This drives rates high," he said.
Cheserem urged commercial banks to educate customers on the need to pay back loans because currently, "borrowing is like a big wedding party, paying back like a funeral."
He saw low overseas borrowing keeping demand for domestic resources high. Cheserem said proposed amendments in the Central Bank of Kenya Act would raise confidence to borrow overseas.
An official from the central bank said commercial banks still appeared unjustified in charging high interest rates despite the central bank's high offers for treasury bills.

"The cost of money (for commercial banks) would on average reach just about 15 pErcent. Right now, when you put money in a bank, the highest levels you are paid in interest is around 16-18 percent, so where do they get this 30 percent figure to levy when you borrow?" asked the senior official.
